cases.review: Candidate retains one physical hanging/drooping use, grouping lowered-head posture with it. Baseline timed out; no paired quality comparison exists for this case.

senses.label: hang down or droop
notes: A verb describing something hanging downward or drooping, including a person lowering the head; the same core use covers physical objects and posture.
Common in constructions such as 垂到水面 and 垂着头.

cases.review: Baseline selected a deadline sense illustrated through 过时不候. Candidate retains only outdated/out of fashion, matching the agreed target boundary.

senses.label: outdated; out of fashion
notes: Describes something no longer current, useful, or fashionable, such as technology, ideas, information, or clothing: 这种说法已经过时了.
Often corresponds to “outdated,” “obsolete,” or “old-fashioned,” depending on context.

senses.label: past the appointed time; expired
notes: Means that a specified time or deadline has passed, especially for an appointment, validity period, or rule: 过时不候 means “no waiting after the appointed time.”
This use is more formal or notice-like than “late”; it focuses on being beyond the allowed or scheduled time.

senses.label: outdated; out of fashion
notes: Describes ideas, styles, methods, technology, or things that are no longer current or fashionable.
Commonly used predicatively or before a noun; it can imply that something is obsolete or no longer suitable, not merely old.

cases.review: Candidate retains the degree/change construction. It drops baseline separate have-something-to-pursue use; whether that constitutes a useful distinct target use remains editorial judgment.

senses.label: somewhat; to some extent
notes: A formal written pattern, usually 所有? no: 有所 + verb or adjective, indicating a limited change, effect, difference, or improvement.
Common in news, formal speech, and practical writing; it often corresponds to “show some improvement” or “be somewhat different,” rather than a strong degree.

senses.label: have something to do, pursue, or possess
notes: A more literary or bound-form use in patterns such as 有所作为, 有所追求, or 各有所好, where 所 nominalizes the following action or quality.
Useful mainly for recognizing fixed expressions and formal prose; do not normally treat standalone 有所 as an ordinary substitute for 有一些.

senses.label: to some extent; show a certain degree of change
notes: A formal construction meaning that something occurs or changes to an unspecified, usually limited degree, as in 有所改善 or 有所不同.
Typically used before a verb or adjective and is more common in careful speech and writing than in casual conversation.

cases.review: Candidate retains inability-to-bear and post-adjective extreme-degree constructions. Baseline third unfit/incapable grouping disappears; this is consistent with reducing close divisions but not independently verified exhaustiveness.

senses.label: cannot bear or withstand
notes: Verb-like and usually formal; means being unable to endure a person, burden, situation, or action.
Common constructions include 不堪忍受, 不堪其扰, 不堪重负, and 不堪回首.

senses.label: unbearably; extremely
notes: Placed after an adjective to show that a state has reached an excessive or distressing degree, as in 疲惫不堪 and 狼狈不堪.
This is not a fully general everyday intensifier; it is especially common in established descriptive phrases and has a formal or literary tone.

senses.label: unfit for or incapable of
notes: Used in compact formal constructions for something that cannot meet a use, standard, or challenge, as in 不堪一击, 不堪入目, and 不堪大用.
This overlaps with the core idea of not being able to withstand, but the construction focuses on suitability or adequacy rather than personal endurance.

senses.label: cannot bear or withstand
notes: Used in constructions such as 不堪忍受, 不堪回首, and 不堪重负 to mean being unable to endure, tolerate, or withstand something.
Often somewhat formal or literary, but common in both written Chinese and set collocations.

senses.label: extremely; to an unbearable degree
notes: Usually follows a descriptive word, as in 疲惫不堪 or 狼狈不堪, and intensifies an already negative or undesirable state.
The sense is stronger than ordinary 很: it suggests reaching an extreme, often unpleasant, degree.

cases.review: Physical and figurative controls survive. Candidate omits baseline foamed-material use; that may have independent shortened-noun usage and needs review before calling the narrower inventory fully correct.

senses.label: foam or froth
notes: A mass of small bubbles on or in a liquid, such as soap lather, beer foam, or sea foam. It normally refers to the foamy mass rather than one individual bubble; 气泡 is used for a single air bubble.

senses.label: bubble or inflated, short-lived value
notes: A figurative bubble that looks substantial but is fragile, exaggerated, or ultimately unsustainable. Common in economic and social contexts such as 房地产泡沫, 股市泡沫, and 泡沫破裂; it can also describe a hollow or short-lived prosperity more generally, usually with a critical tone.

senses.label: foamed material
notes: A technical or commercial use for lightweight cellular material, especially in compounds such as 泡沫塑料 and 泡沫板. In this sense 泡沫 often functions as a bound or shortened form, so it is useful mainly for recognizing specialized compounds rather than as a default standalone word.

senses.label: Foam or lather
notes: A noun for a mass of small bubbles on or in a liquid, such as soap lather, shaving foam, or froth.
Used for a visible, usually temporary layer or accumulation of bubbles in ordinary concrete contexts.

senses.label: Speculative or inflated bubble
notes: A figurative noun for an overinflated, fragile situation or asset market whose apparent value is not sustainable.
Common in economic and financial discussion, especially with property, housing, or stock markets; it emphasizes the bubble's instability and eventual risk of bursting.

cases.review: Concrete seasoning use remains, with dish names illustrating the ingredient rather than becoming new component senses. Botanical detail in generated notes was not independently verified.

senses.label: green Sichuan pepper
notes: A fragrant, citrusy, tongue-tingling peppercorn used as a Sichuan cooking ingredient; it may refer to the fresh or dried spice and to products made from it, such as 藤椒油.
Especially common on menus and in food descriptions, often in compounds such as 藤椒味, 藤椒鸡 and 藤椒鱼.

senses.label: green Sichuan pepper
notes: A fragrant, tongue-tingling Sichuan pepper used as a seasoning, especially in sauces, hot pots, and dishes such as 藤椒鸡. It commonly refers to the fresh green peppercorn or the corresponding dried spice; 藤椒 is more specific than the general 花椒.

cases.review: Baseline retains a grape bound-form sense with defaultUseful false. Candidate returns an empty inventory as expected under the agreed policy.

senses.label: grape (bound form in 葡萄)
notes: 葡 is not normally used as a standalone everyday word; it is the first bound element of 葡萄, “grape,” and related compounds such as 葡萄酒.
The useful vocabulary lies in the compounds, not in learning 葡 as an independent lexical item.

cases.review: Candidate drops baseline 与其-derived rather-than sense and retains conjunction/preposition uses. Literary give/grant is unselected but retained; its notes refer to fixed constructions, so target-level support still needs editorial review.

senses.label: and; as well as
notes: A formal or written conjunction, broadly equivalent to 和 or 以及. Common in formal prose, titles, announcements, and set phrases, but less natural than 和 in ordinary conversation.

senses.label: with; to; in relation to
notes: A formal preposition marking association, comparison, interaction, or a recipient, as in 与他合作, 与现实相比, and 与用户沟通. It often corresponds to 和, 跟, or 对 in colloquial speech.

senses.label: rather than (与其……不如……)
notes: A common fixed comparison pattern meaning “rather than A, it is better to B.” 与其 normally appears with 不如, 宁可, or a similar contrasting expression; the construction is somewhat formal but useful in speech and writing.

senses.label: give; grant; transfer
notes: A formal, literary, or classical verb meaning “give,” “grant,” or “transfer,” retained mainly in fixed expressions and compounds such as 赠与 and 授与. Do not confuse it with the modern everyday verb 给.

senses.label: and; as well as
notes: Conjunction linking nouns, noun phrases, or clauses. More formal and written than 和 or 跟, but common in formal prose and set grammatical patterns.

senses.label: with; together with; in relation to
notes: Preposition introducing a companion, counterpart, or party in a relationship, comparison, cooperation, or interaction. Frequent in formal and written Mandarin; everyday speech usually prefers 和 or 跟.

senses.label: give; grant
notes: A literary or classical verb meaning to give or grant. It survives in some compact formal or fixed constructions, but is not the normal modern standalone verb for everyday 'give'; use 给 for that meaning.
